svg.text: Frailty: why a small insult produces a large collapse
The illness is often trivial. The reserve is what is missing.
The same event, two different people
A urinary infection in a fit 40-year-old: burning, frequency, a course of antibiotics, back to work
The same infection in a frail 82-year-old: sudden confusion, a fall, unable to stand, admitted
Nothing about the infection differs. What differs is what was left in reserve.
So the presenting problem is a fall or confusion, and the diagnosis is somewhere else entirely
The five presentations that hide a cause
Sudden confusion
A fall, or several falls
Not eating, or a sudden loss of weight
New incontinence in someone who was dry
Taking to the bed and stopping walking
Each one is a symptom, never a diagnosis
What to look for underneath
Infection, most often chest or urine
A new medicine, or a dose that is now too big
Dehydration, constipation, retention of urine
Pain that nobody has asked about
Low sodium, low glucose, a silent heart attack
Start with the bladder and the drug chart
The temperature that is not there
An older person with serious infection is often afebrile, and may be hypothermic instead
A normal temperature does not exclude sepsis. Behaviour changes before the thermometer does.
